Information Provided

We are told the data file contains these columns expressing the following CPU characteristics:

  • MYCT: machine cycle time in nanoseconds (integer)
  • MbMIN: minimum main memory in kilobytes (integer)
  • MMAX: maximum main memory in kilobytes (integer)
  • CACH: cache memory in kilobytes (integer)
  • CHMIN: minimum channels in units (integer)
  • CHMAX: maximum channels in units (integer)
  • PRP: published relative performance (integer) (target variable)

Upon loading the data file to df we can see there are 7 columns where the above feature names were assigned as corresponding headers, all columns are in fact integer class typre, and there are 209 observations. From the str( ) head( ) and summary( ) the values of each column appear to be discrete categories with numeric magnitude that is relevant, and the count of how many unique values are present for each feature does indicate discrete and somewhat limited categories

Looking at outputs, the ‘Mean’ is roughly \(2\times\) larger than the ‘Median’ with a range of all ‘positive’ values. This typically indicates a ‘non-normal’ distribution (either that or it has extreme values). But the glimpse of values observed in the data from these features seem to have a multiplicative of 4 distinction to me so the distribution is unknown immediately and visualization of the data would help determine distribution and any relationship. Especially if this is taken into consideration when looking at the ‘Mean’ values that are relatively in the middle of ‘1st Qu.’ and ’3rd Qu.’values. Lastly, there are 2 ‘NA’ values in the feature ‘CHMIN’.

2.4 Shapiro-Wilks Test for Normality

#initialize list 
norm.list <- vector("list", length = ncol(df))

for(c in 1:ncol(df)){
  norm.list[[c]] <- temp <- shapiro.test(df[,c])
  print(paste0("Column '", names(df)[c], "' has a W statistic = ", round(temp$statistic, 3), " and p-value = ", formatC(temp$p.value, digits = 3, format = 'fg')))
}
## [1] "Column 'MYCT' has a W statistic = 0.663 and p-value = 0.0000000000000000000376"
## [1] "Column 'MbMIN' has a W statistic = 0.612 and p-value = 0.00000000000000000000171"
## [1] "Column 'MMAX' has a W statistic = 0.758 and p-value = 0.0000000000000000308"
## [1] "Column 'CACH' has a W statistic = 0.646 and p-value = 0.0000000000000000000125"
## [1] "Column 'CHMIN' has a W statistic = 0.566 and p-value = 0.000000000000000000000182"
## [1] "Column 'CHMAX' has a W statistic = 0.597 and p-value = 0.000000000000000000000753"
## [1] "Column 'PRP' has a W statistic = 0.558 and p-value = 0.000000000000000000000095"

Based on the Shapiro-Wilks Test for normality where a W statistic closer to 1 indicates a distribution reflective of normal distribution a p-value < 0.05 means that the ‘null hypothesis’ for a normal distribution is rejected. Because most “W” statistics are closer to 0.5 than 1.0 and the p-values are significantly below 0.05, the null is rejected for normality. This means transformations will be needed to make a multiple-linear regression model.

2.5 Correlation Benchmark for Untransformed Data

pairs.panels(df)


The function pairs.panels( ) confirms the non-linear relation of features due to the left-skews and non-normal distribution. Looking at the data values following a pattern of doubling (i.e. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) seems to indicate \(x = 2^{y}\) which would be transformed using \(\log_2( feature )\) and likely a transformation outside of ‘Channel’ values which are more sequential in value.

Relevant Domain Knowledge

Because I have limited domain knowledge with CPU components etc, I did some investigation on the features presented in order to appropriately handle Missing Values and Outliers.I believe some information about the units of measure for digital data should be noted, especially that conversions of digital data have constant relationships and a ‘bit’ is the smallest unit of data that can only be represented by a 0 or 1 1.

MbMAX, MMAX, CACH

Base measures:

  • nano (n) = \(10^{9}\)
  • kilo (k) = \(10^{3}\)
  • mega (M) = \(10^{6}\)
  • Byte (B) = 8 Bits 2

Digital Data Conversions where kilbytes is indicated as the unit for memory associated columns:

  • 1 kB 3 = 0.001 MB = 1024 Bytes = 8192 bits
  • 1 MB = 1,000 kB
  • 1 ns = 0.000000001 s = \(1\times10^{-9}\)s
PRP*, CHMIN, CHMAX, MYCT:
  • CPU 4 = central processing unit
  • PRP is relative performance and target but : Computer performance5 is the amount of useful work accomplished by a computer system
  • CHMIN & CHMAX : Channels 6 have their capacity as additive over independent channels
  • MYCT : Cycle Time 7 is how long it takes to process a given job

3. Missing Values

Even though str() indicated there were 2 Missing Values in ‘CHMIN’, we will iterate over columns using which(); borrowing approach from Module 07.5 by Professor Schedlbauer. However only the numeric strategy of is.na( ) is needed as no string values are present in df.

#initialize object as false for print 
found <- F

for(c in 1:ncol(df)){
  missing.Values <- which(is.na(df[,c]))
  num.Missing.Values <- length(missing.Values)
  if(num.Missing.Values > 0){
    print(paste0("Column '", names(df)[c], "' has ", num.Missing.Values, " missing values"))
    found <- T
  }
}
## [1] "Column 'CHMIN' has 2 missing values"

With only 2 NA values in the entire data set and within the same column, it seems the values are ‘Missing Completely at Random’ and should be imputed. The method of feature average was discouraged, so I think the exploration of kNN, kNN regression, Model Regression Tree, Decision Tree, and Naive Bayes are the potential options for imputation.

kNN and Decision Tree are non-parametric, while Naive Bayes is reasonably parametric but has amplified combined predictive effect for categories. I explored all of these methods except the binned Decision Tree. I will mainly explain my choice with limited code on the rejected methods.

The features are integers, meaning they are numeric in value but they can be ‘binned’ into discrete categories easily.

Continuous Regression (not selected)

I did attempt numeric regression where a continuous variable was returned by either kNN Regression or Model Regression Tree where various ‘k’ and ‘cp’ values were explored respectively. Overall, accuracy was roughly 50% where despite a high cor( ) value of approximately 0.88; but there are many ‘bins’ and the numeric magnitude of the feature does have importance for impact on pairing with other features. Because of dense clustering of lower magnitude values the continuous variable return had large error/high variance even attempting to select the closest ‘discrete category’. If scaling was not performed first , which is unusual for kNN, the predictions were basically the same as the scaled.

Discrete Classification (Naive Bayes Selected)

Again, just scaling features to utilize the non-parametric methods of kNN or Decision Tree had a rough accuracy of 50% with low ‘kappa’. Due to this and the relatively low correlation found before any transformations, it made the idea of transforming to a relatively normal distribution and utilizing the amplified prediction power of Naive Bayes for low impact features a better approach. After visual inspection of all model predictions and validation sets, Naive Bayes seemed the more accurate even if the ‘accuracy’ percents were similar. That has to do with the naive nature of the mode, but therefore the method I selected Naive Bayes Classification for imputation of missing values.

3. Imputation by Naive Bayes Classification

Naive Bayes assumptions:

  • relatively normal distribution
  • independent variables (not necessarily true but currently low correlation)
  • equal importance of variables (so even small impact will contribute to classification)
  • works best for categorical data (so need to ‘re-categorize’ after transformation)

General handling for Data Models:

I will treat the numeric values as ordinal features with ranked order based on the min-max scaled value.

Since PRP is the overall goal and the relation is not defined, and overfitting should be avoided; the column ‘PRP’ with be excluded for the model predictions for ‘CHMIN’. The NA values (rows : 31 , 170 are the ultimate goal so they will also be removed from the training and testing sets.

# data frames for missing value imputation
targets <- which(is.na(df$CHMIN))
# remove PRP for CHMIN imputation
df.nb <- df[, -which(colnames(df) == 'PRP')]

3.1 Normalize the Data for Naive Bayes

#initialize data frame for log_2 transformation
df.log2 <- df.nb
# log(1, base = 2) = 0
for(col in 1:ncol(df.log2)) {
  min_val <- min(df.nb[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  if (min_val <= 0) {
    shift <- abs(min_val) + 0.99
    df.log2[[col]] <- log(df.nb[[col]] + shift, base = 2)
  } else {
    df.log2[[col]] <- log(df.nb[[col]], base = 2)
  }
}

pairs.panels(df.log2)

3.2 Scale Up and Factor for Naive Bayes Categorical Use

With the log(base = 2) transformation the data became normalized, however this is a very condensed range for all features with the target ‘CHMIN’ range [NA , NA]. After much trial , error, and investigation into factor( ). I learned that factor will preserve “numeric” values as “integers”. With the transformation there are multiple categories that would have the same integer value. So in order to maintain this transformation of normality but facilitate the need for distinct categories, I am scaling the values up by a factor of 100 for use in Naive Bayes Modeling.

# transformations for use as factors
df.nb <- as.data.frame(lapply(df.log2, round, digit = 3))
df.nb.scale <- 100 * df.nb

# categorical data.frame for nb.model
df.nbf <- as.data.frame(lapply(df.nb.scale, as.factor))

# maintains some shape when scaled
pairs.panels(df.nb.scale)

3.3 Lookup Factor Values in Data Frame

With the creation of data.frame copies to manipulated for each transformation of the data, a 1:1 index of values can be used for look up to impute predicted value.

# CHMIN target

chminF2 <- as.data.frame(lapply(chminF, function(x){sort(unique(x))}))

3.4 Test Transformed and Scaled Data’s Normality to satisfy Naive Bayes Assumption

#initialize list 
norm.list.scale <- vector("list", length = ncol(df.nb.scale))

for(c in 1:ncol(df.log2)){
  norm.list.scale[[c]] <- temp <- shapiro.test(df.nb.scale[,c])
  print(paste0("Column '", names(df.nb.scale)[c], "' has a W statistic = ", round(temp$statistic, 3), " and p-value = ", formatC(temp$p.value, digits = 3, format = 'fg')))
}
## [1] "Column 'MYCT' has a W statistic = 0.967 and p-value = 0.000086"
## [1] "Column 'MbMIN' has a W statistic = 0.973 and p-value = 0.000533"
## [1] "Column 'MMAX' has a W statistic = 0.958 and p-value = 0.00000701"
## [1] "Column 'CACH' has a W statistic = 0.881 and p-value = 0.00000000000942"
## [1] "Column 'CHMIN' has a W statistic = 0.864 and p-value = 0.00000000000121"
## [1] "Column 'CHMAX' has a W statistic = 0.982 and p-value = 0.00997"

Here we can see that the data after transformation is significantly closer to a normal distribution (maintained in scaled data) based on the Shapiro-Wilk’s W statistic being very close to 1. While the p-value is below 0.05 to reject the null hypothesis of normal distribution this is significantly closer. So proceeding with Naive Bayes to impute the missing value is good. Also these methods will be used to transform. the multiple linear regression model.

I will note I spent way longer than I should have to realize the \(x =2^{y}\) distribution and ended up testing gamma, exponential, natural log, and did so with caret and e107. I tried cross validations, Box-Cox (my backup), I did sqrt() into log() base e (my very first approach - so at least intuitively I was kinda there), PCA, and then realized log base 2. I finally realized the log should have base 2 because I remember Professor Schedlbauer’s Lecture The C5.0 Algorith, where he comments that ‘in computer science we always use base two’. But I got there eventually.

I chose the model approach of Naive Bayes based on data transformed by sqrt() and then natural log() (double transformation). But also I learned through much trial and error how factor( ) works for the re categorization of the levels and labels, where integer values are what results so the same relative distribution is maintained for the label but the digits of precision is lost. Meaning the ‘normality’ is not quite as good but that’s okay since Naive Bayes works best on categorical data and it only needs reasonably normal data.

3.5 Split the Data for Naive Bayes Model Testing

Intentionally left warning here, to highlight that some values aren’t present in data sets.

# reproducible results
set.seed(16) 
#remove NA targets
df.nbf2 <- df.nbf[-targets,]

#index for training and validation
split.index <- createDataPartition(df.nbf2$CHMIN,
                                   p = 0.8,
                                   list = FALSE)
## Warning in createDataPartition(df.nbf2$CHMIN, p = 0.8, list = FALSE): Some
## classes have a single record ( 299.8, 464.3, 475.4, 504.4 ) and these will be
## selected for the sample
# testing (t) and validation (v) sets
nb.t <- df.nbf2[split.index,]
nb.v <- df.nbf2[-split.index,]

# labels for t & v sets
factor.t <- df.nbf2[split.index, 'CHMIN']
factor.v <- df.nbf2[-split.index, 'CHMIN']

3.6 Build Naive Bayes Model and Evaluate Accuracy

nb.model <- naiveBayes(CHMIN ~.,
                       data = nb.t,
                       laplace = 0.000001)

nb.prediction <- predict(nb.model,
                         newdata = nb.v[,-which(colnames(nb.v) == 'CHMIN')])

#accuracy
cM_nb.model <- confusionMatrix(nb.prediction, factor.v)
cM_nb.model$overall['Accuracy']
##  Accuracy 
## 0.6944444
cM_nb.model$overall['Kappa']
##     Kappa 
## 0.5690968

This is actually a really decent model (especially considering all other models were returning an accuracy near 50% with a Kappa near 0.25 for most of my previous attempts). I will use this to predict the missing ‘CHMIN’ values and look up the prediction’s corresponding labels to impute.

5. Handling Outliers

Again a majority of these values are actually categorical in nature where magnitude increases make sense. So Rather the values should be evaluated with that in mind and the columns described units of measure previously discussed. So normalization of the data should be done first, since outliers are evaluations of empirical distribution norms. Which is by a log_2 transformation method identified previously.

Unlike the previous scaling though, ‘0.01’ instead of ‘0.99’ will be used for any zeros in the data set to avoid ‘-Inf’ return but maintain 0 as a distinct value and not part of values transformed that were 1.

5.1 Normalize all Data for Outlier Evaluation

# df of All transformed data
dfA.log2 <- df
# log(1, base = 2) = 0
for(col in 1:ncol(dfA.log2)) {
  min_val <- min(df[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  if (min_val <= 0) {
    shift <- abs(min_val) + 0.01
    dfA.log2[[col]] <- log(df[[col]] + shift, base = 2)
  } else {
    dfA.log2[[col]] <- log(df[[col]], base = 2)
  }
}

pairs.panels(dfA.log2)

5.2 Identify Outliers by z-Score

Borrow logic and printing from Module 07.5 by Professor Schedlbauer.

#create z-score matrix of transformed values
df.z <- as.data.frame(lapply(dfA.log2, scale))
# loop print
for (c in 1:ncol(df.z)) {
  # outliers
  outliers <- which(abs(df.z[,c]) > 3.0)
  #print statements
  if (length(outliers) > 0) {
    ## found outliers; replace with NA and impute later
    cat("Found ", length(outliers), " outliers in column '", names(df)[c], "': \n")
    cat("   --> ", df[outliers,c], "\n")
  }
}

5.7 Calculated ‘MbMIN’ Value From ‘MMAX’

# integer vector of Multipliers
multiplier <- as.integer(df[-mbmin.out, 'MMAX'] / df[-mbmin.out, 'MbMIN'])
avg.mult <- mean(multiplier)
# vector of unique multipliers
mode.mult <- sort(unique(multiplier))
# initialize the count vector for multipliers found
count.mode <- vector(length = length(mode.mult))
# tally counts
for(i in 1:length(count.mode)){
  count.mode[i] <- length(which(multiplier == mode.mult[i]))
}
# data.frame of counts to multiplier
mode.df <- data.frame(count = count.mode, 
                      multiplier = mode.mult)
# find maximum count of multiplier used
mode.index <- which(mode.df$count == max(mode.df$count))
mode.found <- mode.df[mode.index,'multiplier']
mode.found
## [1] 4

Use Mode of Multiplicative Factor between ‘MbMIN’ & ‘MMAX’ = 4

Because of the strong correlation between the channel columns and the multiplicative/scaled relationship I felt was present, I decided to find the mode of the multiplier in the data and use that to calculate the corresponding ‘MbMIN’ values. I did investigate how many columns had equal Memory min and max but it was very infrequent so I felt confident in this approach.

After looking at the data, it appears that ‘MbMIN’ and ‘MMAX’ have a scaled relationship. I divided all other ‘MMAX’ by ‘MbMIN’ with result coerced to integer. Found the resultant mode multiplier. Then divided the outlier’s corresponding ‘MMAX’ by that multiplier to impute for the outlier in ‘MbMIN’

5.8 Impute MbMIN Value = 16000

df[mbmin.out, 'MbMIN'] <- df[mbmin.out, 'MMAX']/mode.found
df[mbmin.out,]

After evaluating the ‘MbMIN’ column I did not have confidence to exclude 96 as an outlier by using a ‘2.5’ z-Score, so I only lowered the z-Score to ‘2.9’. Most observations do not have the ‘MbMIN’ == ‘MMAX’, by they do appear to be a factor relation, and the pairs.panel( ) supports a strong correlation.

Therefore, I think treating the outlier for row 15 in ‘MbMIN’ should be treated as a missing value to impute.

Multiplicative Mode found = 4 with a count of 62, used to calculate ‘MbMIN’ imputed value 1.6^{4}

6. Normalize df with \(\log_2\) for Regression

Normalization wil be by \(\log_2\) as previously stated for the previously imputed values. But I will use shift = ‘0.50’ instead of ‘0.01’ or ‘0.99’, because it results in “-1” which is the same different in value as \(\log_2{1} \text{ and } \log_2{2}\). This is because the ‘CACH’, ‘CHMIN’, and ‘CHMAX’ all have ‘0’ values that I confirmed as valid possibilities for those categories and since $_2(0) = Inf $ I felt a shift was necessary.

df.norm <- df
# log(1, base = 2) = 0
for(col in 1:ncol(df.norm)) {
  min_val <- min(df.norm[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  if (min_val <= 0) {
    shift <- abs(min_val) + 0.5
    df.norm[[col]] <- log(df[[col]] + shift, base = 2)
  } else {
    df.norm[[col]] <- log(df[[col]], base = 2)
  }
}

pairs.panels(df.norm)

Like previously stated there is a very strong correlation for multiple features. Based on the correlation Matrix, I would say all values that at 0.70 and above have a strong correlation.

Multicollinearities between Predictor Features

  1. CHMIN to CHMAX
  2. MbMIN to MMAX
  3. MYCT to MbMIN

Features with a strong Correlation to PRP target:

  1. MYCT (negative)
  2. MbMIN
  3. MMAX
  4. CACH

It makes since for min and max of the same feature to have a strong correlation because directly impact what value the other one can have(i.e. minimum can’t exceed the maximum). Just like the relationship between cycle time and available memory makes sense

I personally believe removing the minimum values would make the most sense to avoid multimillionaires in the data, since the maximum Channels or Memory possible would limit the CPU’s overall performance as a ceiling threshold basically the computer is unable to exceed a certain level of performance.

I would choose to explore multiple iteration where I’d starting with removing ‘MbMIN’ and ‘CHMIN’ but with the use of all features into step-wise backward regression by p-value and step() for AIC you will see that those are actually both left in the model, but the resultant model has multicollinearity as a result (which is bad because it leads to overfitting).

9.3 Resultant Multiple Linear Regression Model

lm(formula = PRP ~ MbMIN + MMAX + CACH + CHMIN, data = reg.t)

r.m <- summary(reg.fit3)
b0 <- r.m$coefficients[[1]] # intercept
b1 <- r.m$coefficients[[2]] # MbMIN 
b2 <- r.m$coefficients[[3]] # MMAX
b3 <- r.m$coefficients[[4]] # CACH
b4 <- r.m$coefficients[[5]] # CHMIN

plugin <- function(df){
  predictions <- vector(length= nrow(df))
  for(r in 1:nrow(df)){
    b1_plug <- df[r, which(colnames(df) == 'MbMIN')]
    b2_plug <- df[r, which(colnames(df) == 'MMAX')]
    b3_plug <- df[r, which(colnames(df) == 'CACH')]
    b4_plug <- df[r, which(colnames(df) == 'CHMIN')]
    predictions[r] <- b0 + (b1 * b1_plug) + (b2 * b2_plug) + (b3 * b3_plug) + (b4 * b4_plug)
  }
  predictions
}

\[ PRP = (0.234 \times \text{MbMIN}) + (0.437 \times \text{MMAX}) + (0.072 \times \text{CACH})+ (0.111 \times \text{CHMIN}) - 2.530 \] Where:
\(\beta_1\) = 0.1642242
\(\beta_2\) = 0.405353
\(\beta_3\) = 0.1544348
\(\beta_4\) = 0.258559
\(\beta_0\) = -2.0157186

10. Evaluate Model Performance

Funnily enough, the resultant model is the complete opposite of what my initial impression was for feature selection. But all features have a p value less that 0.05 and considered significant contributors to the model.

\(R^{2}\) = 0.8030006
\(\text{Adjusted}\;R^{2}\) = 0.7984457

Indicating that the model does a reasonably good job at representing the data set, with 79.8% variance in the data set explained by the Multiple Linear Regression Model.

rmse.fit3 <- sqrt(mse.fit3)

11. New Data Point:

df.new.data <- data.frame(MYCT = 180,
                       MbMIN = 262, 
                       MMAX = 4000,
                       CACH = 0.50, # avoid log_2 of 0 = -Inf
                       CHMIN = 1,
                       CHMAX = 3)
# transform
new.dl2 <- as.data.frame(lapply(df.new.data, log, base = 2))

# prediction/CI of transformed data.point
new.conf <- predict(reg.fit3, 
                    newdata = new.dl2, 
                    interval = 'confidence')
# undo transformation
new.conf2 <- sapply(new.conf, function(x){2^x})

# plugin method double check
plugin(new.dl2)
## [1] 3.999495

However this was the \(y = \log_2{x}\) transformation; in order to get the same unit value as the original data frame and new data point a reverse transformation needs to take place using \(x = 2^{y}\)

Conclusion:

I used all features to start due to the Canvas Assignment instructions, but in real-world practice, I would not due to the high multicollinearity previously identified that subsequently got built into the final model by step-wise backward elimination and minimum AIC, so while these graphs and numbers look great; they indicate overfitting to the data set and would likely do poorly for other data. While the digital relationship of conversion is constant there are some questions on the low end value input accuracy and the amplified impact of some features on the target ‘PRP’.
